title: Hazel and the Radiators
premise: Coral Ishikawa, a piano tuner in a fading mill town, has spent thirty years cataloguing what her family never said—her grandmother's silence, her father's exile, the unrecorded song her uncle wrote before disappearing. When she hears that song playing on a late-night radio broadcast, credited to a stranger, she realizes someone survived and someone profited. Tracing the broadcast to a dying record producer, Coral must decide whether justice means exposure or inheritance, and whether the woman in the old photographs—the one everyone called a liar—deserves her forgiveness. In the end, Coral records the song herself, gives it back to the family that was robbed of it, and lets the house go cold on purpose.
about_author: Casper Vasquez is the pen name of a former building superintendent who spent a decade listening to the pipes of pre-war apartment houses. Their essays on sound, tenancy, and family debt have appeared in small literary journals under three other names.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Coral, tuning the piano in her late grandmother's boarded-up house, introduces her habit of keeping a ledger of silences: the locked bedroom, the missing photograph, the song her uncle Toshi wrote that no one will name. POV: Coral, first person. Emotional beat: tender, controlled grief dressed up as professional competence.

chapters.title: Static at 2 A.M.
chapters.summary: Unable to sleep, Coral hears a late-night jazz program play a melody she knows note for note—Toshi's unfinished song, broadcast under another composer's name. She tapes the broadcast and compares it to the hum she remembers from the radiators. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: vertigo; the past has broken its seal.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Coral searches the house's walls and finds her grandmother's letters to a lawyer, never sent, alleging that a bandmate stole Toshi's compositions after his death. The radiators, she realizes, carry the house's memory—knocks, expansion, the rhythm of someone pacing. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: the thrill of evidence and the guilt of digging.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Photographs
chapters.summary: In a shoebox, Coral studies photos of her grandmother with a smiling man—Marcus Vale, the bandmate—whose face she has hated her whole life without knowing why. Her father, reached by phone, refuses to talk and hangs up. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: inherited anger meeting its first complication.

chapters.title: A Visit to Vale Records
chapters.summary: Coral travels to the city and gets a job tuning the piano at Vale's studio, where she discovers the aging producer Marcus Vale is dying and hoarding master tapes—including one labeled with Toshi's real name. POV: Coral, with a shift into close third on Vale. Emotional beat: predatory patience; Coral realizes she is capable of scheming.

chapters.title: The Man in the Oxygen Mask
chapters.summary: Vale, sensing Coral's interest in the tapes, tells her a version of the past: Toshi sold the songs willingly, and the grandmother's 'theft' story was grief rewritten. He offers Coral money for her silence. POV: Vale's confession framed through Coral. Emotional beat: the ground tilts; the villain becomes a narrator.

chapters.title: Ledger of Doubts
chapters.summary: Coral cross-examines the letters, the tape labels, and her own memory of the radiators' rhythm, and finds her grandmother's story has seams—Toshi was desperate, ill, and signed something. Her father finally calls back and admits he knew. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: betrayal compounded; the family's silence protected a lie on both sides.

chapters.title: The Last Session
chapters.summary: Vale, near death, summons Coral to hear the full master recording: Toshi's voice, singing his own song, followed by a spoken message for 'the girl who tunes pianos'—he knew his sister would come someday. Vale asks not for forgiveness but for a witness. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: the climax; grief, rage, and recognition in a single room.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Coral declines the settlement and the lawsuit both. Instead she engineers exposure on her own terms: she leaks Toshi's voice to a music historian, secures the copyright through his estate, and lets Vale die knowing the record will carry the right name. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: cold, deliberate, and strangely peaceful—justice as authorship, not punishment.

chapters.title: Letting the House Go Cold
chapters.summary: Coral records the song herself in the empty house, one take, radiators knocking in the background, and mails copies to her father and the archive. She forgives the strangers in the photographs—her grandmother, her uncle, even Vale—and shuts off the boiler for winter. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: release; the inventory of unsaid things finally closes.
